• Common name: Mexican oak leaf (also spring-run whitehead)
  • Scientific name: Shinnersia rivularis (previously Trichocoronis rivularis)
  • Difficulty: easy to moderate
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • pH: 5.0–8.0
  • GH: 2–16
  • Temperature: 15–30°C
  • Substrate: any
  • Can be grown emersed: yes
  • Growth rate: fast
  • Placement: midground and background
  • Height: 15–30 cm
  • CO2: not needed
  • Propagation: by cuttings
  • Colour: green

This plant is native to isolated aquatic systems in Mexico and the southwestern region of Texas.

In Mexico it occurs in northern Coahuila and northern Nuevo León. In Texas, its presence is limited to two locations along the Nueces River in Uvalde County, two sites in Kinney County, and San Felipe Springs and San Felipe Creek in Del Rio, Val Verde County.

It is now cultivated globally as an aquarium plant and has expanded beyond its native range, becoming established even in Europe (thermal waters of Austria, Hungary, Germany and Slovakia). Some reports suggest it has been found in the wild in Australia, but it is not yet naturalized there.
Shinnersia rivularis grows emersed or submersed in shallow (0.3–1 m) slow-moving warm waters. It is not found in deep waters.

The recommended minimum tank size is about 40 litres. Because of its growth potential, tall tanks are better than long tanks. In short tanks it reaches the top very fast and starts trailing along the surface.

In aquariums it is used as a classic stem plant, planted along the sides, in the midground or background due to its larger size.

Be ready to trim it often, since it grows fast even in low light. Once established, it may take only a few weeks before it is ready for propagation or trimming.

Do not allow the plant to reach the surface, or you may get a big tangled mass. Start trimming when there are 10–15 cm left to the water surface. You can safely shorten it by half; it grows back quickly. Trim regularly to prevent overcrowding and promote bushier growth.

Planting

Plant stems about 5 cm apart. A solitary stem looks thin and elongated, while groups give a full, lush look. The plant eventually forms extensive mats, so make sure it does not shade other plants. Simply plant it deep enough in the substrate to keep it from floating up; tweezers can be used.

Propagation

It propagates vegetatively by cuttings and side shoots. Cut the upper portion of the stem with sharp scissors just above a leaf node; ideal cuttings are about 10 cm long. Make a hole in the substrate about 3–4 cm deep, place the stems in it and cover with substrate. The new stems develop roots and grow into new plants very fast.

Constant trimming often leads to numerous side shoots whose leaves can be considerably smaller than on the original plant. To keep the plant attractive, uproot it and replant the tops in the same place so the leaves remain large and striking.

Temperature: it thrives in a broad range of 15–30°C, making it suitable for cold-water aquariums. Growth is significantly faster in warmer water.

pH: prefers 6.0–8.0.

Hardness: adaptable to a range of hardness values (2–16 GH), but it grows faster in softer water.

Flow: in nature it grows in slow-flowing water, so a gentle current is optimal.

Lighting: moderate to high light and a photoperiod of 10–12 hours daily are best. It can still adapt and grow well in low-tech tanks, but with insufficient light the stem elongates and density decreases.

Substrate: very undemanding; it grows in almost anything (sand, gravel, etc.), needing only 2.5–5 cm depth. It can even grow floating until it finds a place to anchor and develop roots; when floating, the leaves become noticeably smaller. It absorbs nutrients from the water column and roots at the same time.

CO2: optional. CO2 promotes growth significantly, but a pressurized system is not mandatory.

Fertilization: if the substrate is not nutrient-rich, regular dosing of liquid fertilizer (2–3 times a week) is recommended.

If you keep shrimp with this plant, note that high CO2 levels and copper (many fertilizers contain copper) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Description

A perennial, long-stemmed plant that can be grown partially emersed (paludarium) or fully submersed. In aquariums it usually stands 15–30 cm tall and spreads 10–15 cm; in nature the stem may reach 1 m, about 3 mm thick. Leaves are opposite, attached directly to the stem, with a broad oblanceolate or three-lobed shape, mostly 2–4 cm long. Colour varies from light green to brownish-red in bright light. Under optimal lighting it develops distinctive white veins; the Dennerle nursery developed this form as Shinnersia rivularis 'Weiss-Grün'. Flowers appear above water, with white petals about 2 mm long.

Taxonomy

In 1849 Asa Gray classified it as Trichocoronis rivularis. King and Robinson separated it into the genus Shinnersia in 1970, and a 2014 molecular study further supported the distinction. The genus is named after botanist Lloyd Herbert Shinners; 'rivularis' derives from Latin for a small stream or brook.

Benefits

  • Dense mats provide cover and shade for invertebrates and small fish.
  • Biofilm on it is an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • It takes up phosphorus and nitrogen, and has been reported to remove nutrients, heavy metals and organic contaminants.
  • It outcompetes algae and cyanobacteria for nutrients.

Common problems

  • Overgrowth: under high light and CO2 it can fill the tank within weeks and needs a lot of trimming.
  • Leggy stems: when stems reach the surface or light is insufficient, leaf spacing increases. Check the light, trim, or place it behind driftwood or rocks to hide bare stems.
  • Pale leaves: often a sign of iron deficiency; supplement with mineral fertilizers.

Quarantine

Unless you are sure the plant is safe (e.g. grown in vitro in an unopened, undamaged pot), quarantine and disinfect it before adding it to the tank. It may carry parasites, pests such as snails, predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs), or pesticide residues that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

In the wild it can be invasive, labelled a 'super weed', and researchers have suggested banning it to prevent spread. It suits beginners and can be used in summer ponds, paludariums and aquariums, but needs frequent replanting and thinning.
